title: Towards FAIR industrial data: How semantic metadata management enablesinteroperability for Digital Threads and Digital Twins
items.abstract: <jats:p>Industrial manufacturing faces increasing product and process complexity, combined with the need for shorter development cycles. As a result, data management systems must support interoperable and semantically consistent information representation and exchange. Existing commercial solutions often fail to meet these requirements outside proprietary ecosystems, particularly when shared data models and common semantics are needed. This limits theexplicit representation of domain knowledge and hinders efficient collaboration across system boundaries. This work proposes a system architecture for a semantically enriched data catalog that organizes datasets and their intra- and inter-object metadata to make them findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). The architecture adds a semantic layer on top of a conventional file storage and can be integrated into existing data management systems. A modular domain ontology and complementing Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL) restrictions are utilized as data model for a property graph database to ensure data quality. The resulting knowledge graph increases the value and expressiveness of stored datasets by formalizing the available metadata. This enables the export of selected graph excerpts as RDF for sharing purposes. It also provides a consistent semantic basis for dynamic graphical user interfaces and advanced Digital Twin applications. While the approach enhances transparency and interoperability of industrial data assets, topics that address governance structures and mechanisms for cross-organizational file transfer are notdirectly addressed.</jats:p>

title: Ground-Truthing Latency Alpha: An Independent Test of LLM-Semantic-Extraction Alpha in EIA-Driven Crude Oil Futures
items.abstract: <jats:p>Pape (2025) reports that real-time LLM-based semantic extraction of the EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report yields a tradeable, low-latency signal in crude oil futures (Sharpe ~1.82). We test this thesis independently on a retail capital-efficient stack by decomposing it into two falsifiable sub-claims: (A) a measurable post-release alpha that decays rapidly (the "latency" claim), and (B) that a multi-field / semantic read of the whole report outperforms a single-crude-inventory-surprise number (the "semantic richness" claim). Our method is staged by cost, where a zero-cost parallel observer captures the second-to-minute reaction at each live release; a near-zero-cost historical tick data study measures the sub-second-to-second reaction and its half-life; and an optional low-latency live test estimates the achievable retail capture. The first results (Tier 1, n=10 real EIA releases, CME CL front-month trades) directly test claim (A); the instantaneous release jump captures, on average, only 3.5% of the eventual 30-minute move; the first 30 seconds are net noise (a slight fade), and approximately 40% of the move is realized only by the five-minute mark. Thus, there is no meaningful sub-second repricing to trade crude in this event. A matched placebo control run at scale (149 EIA vs. 146 non-EIA windows over three years) then separates the two questions. In our retail setting, the latency mechanism does not transfer; the instantaneous jump is negligible, and the entry latency across the sub-second-to-30-second range is immaterial. However, the slower minute-scale is genuinely EIA-specific: EIA windows move crude about 1.30x the matched non-EIA windows (Mann-Whitney p = 0.0075), a real if small volatility premium that a smaller ten-release sample had missed as non-significant (p = 0.256), affirming our premise that the release moves the market. We then test whether the premium is directionally harvested. A proxy-consensus screen gives only a faint, non-significant hint (single-crude 57.4%, p = 0.084), and a direct implementation of the semantic method using a language model reading the full multi-field report and issuing a directional call, scored blind over 149 releases does no better (54.1%, p = 0.37) and does not out-predict the single-crude number. We conclude that, for a retail, non-co-located crude/EIA implementation, a tradeable directional edge is not recoverable above chance, most plausibly because the released figures are largely anticipated, which bounds the retail-reachable version and is offered as a complement to, not a contradiction of, the results obtained with institutional infrastructure.</jats:p>

title: Mechanism-Centric Cross-Domain Retrieval for Scientific Discovery: LLM Agents for Structural Isomorphism Beyond Semantic Similarity
items.abstract: <jats:p>Cross-domain isomorphisms, hidden shared structural patterns across disparate fields, are critical for driving interdisciplinary innovation. However, identifying these isomorphisms is difficult due to information overload and knowledge silos. This leaves numerous knowledge connections buried, constraining scientific discovery. To address these limitations, we propose the Mechanism-Centric Cross-Domain Retrieval Framework (MCDF), which integrates three core components: 1) an Expert-Guided Mechanistic Schema with a taxonomy of ten universal mechanism classes, driving 26 domain-specific reasoning agents to generate mechanistically equivalent keywords; 2) a Disentangled Dual-Evaluator architecture that adversarially scores Topic Relevance (TRS) and Mechanism Alignment (MAS) to eliminate metric contamination; and 3) the Isomorphic Serendipity Index (ISI), a novel ranking metric with a cross-domain gain term and a mechanism-gated rarity boost that mathematically incentivizes high mechanistic alignment coupled with maximal semantic distance. In two case studies (social rumor propagation and AI model collapse), MCDF retrieved high-fidelity mechanistic isomorphisms from diverse distant disciplines, average MAS > 0.82 (far higher than BM25 and Deep Research). Results from human evaluation and ablation studies further validate the framework’s effectiveness in enhancing discovery serendipity while maintaining structural validity. MCDF provides a scalable framework for automated cross-domain mining that activates latent knowledge resources to drive interdisciplinary innovation.</jats:p>

title: Semantic Bridges for Student Modeling: Leveraging LLM-Generated Narratives for Interpretable Representation Learning
items.abstract: Student modeling plays a central role in adaptive learning systems. However, current methods often require a trade-off between representational richness and interpretability. Traditional feature engineering produces interpretable but semantically shallow representations, while deep learning methods achieve rich embeddings at the cost of explainability. We propose a framework that utilizes Large Language Model (LLM)-generated narratives as semantic bridges between structured educational data and dense vector representations. Unlike representations learned from scratch, LLM-derived embeddings inherit semantic structure from pretraining on vast text corpora, encoding domain knowledge about education, academic performance, and student success factors. Our approach generates human-readable narratives from student data, then extracts embeddings that preserve both interpretability (through the narrative layer) and computational utility (through dense vectors). We present a comprehensive quality assessment framework evaluating narratives across five dimensions: content quality, linguistic diversity, coherence, uniqueness, and tone appropriateness. Empirical evaluation on 3,169 undergraduate students demonstrates strong content coverage and coherence, with excellent uniqueness.

title: Structure-Guided Retrieval with LLM-Directed Table-of-Contents Navigation and Precomputed Semantic Contagion: A Hybrid RAG Architecture
items.abstract: <jats:p>Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems commonly fail in one of two complementary ways: fine-grained embedding retrieval finds a relevant sentence but returns it stripped of the surrounding context needed to interpret it (the "needle in a haystack" problem), while coarse chunk-based retrieval loses the document's global structure, producing answers that miss the broader picture a question actually calls for. We propose a hybrid RAG architecture that addresses both failure modes simultaneously through three components: (1) an LLM is given a flattened, enriched table of contents (TOC) of the corpus and decides itself which whole sections to retrieve verbatim, exploiting the LLM's structural reasoning rather than embedding similarity; (2) the same LLM call independently proposes several keyword combinations-a principal phrasing plus optional synonym phrasings-each matched independently via its own BM25 query over paragraph-level units, with a per-combination quota governing how many passages each contributes, so that a single dominant concept cannot crowd out the others; (3) within a combination's shortlisted blocks, candidate anchor units are ranked by a threetier lexical-match strength (exact whole-word match of the principal phrasing, of a synonym phrasing, or a partial term match) before being expanded into a coherent, contiguous passage via semantic contagion groups-adjacency chains over sentence-embedding cosine similarity, precomputed entirely offline, so that no vector computation, and no comparison of any embedding against the question or its keywords, occurs at query time. We port the method to FinanceBench [Islam et al., 2023], a public benchmark of real SEC financial filings whose documents exhibit a genuine multi-level section hierarchy and whose gold answers are frequently synthesized, multi-step financial reasoning rather than short extractive spans-a corpus chosen specifically to match the method's design intent, unlike flatter benchmarks with single-sentence answers. On the 150 publicly released FinanceBench questions, our method attains an Answer Accuracy exceeding, and a Page Recall far exceeding, the figures reported by HiREC [Choe et al., 2025], a peer-reviewed hierarchical-retrieval system built on fine-tuned cross-encoders, an iterative complementary-retrieval loop, and a two-model architecture (GPT-4o plus Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct)-while our own architecture uses a single, non-fine-tuned LLM in a single pass. From the composition and weighting of HiREC's own published token-cost table, we further derive a lower bound, exceeding its own reported combined-benchmark average, on its per-query token consumption specifically on FinanceBench-a bound we can only establish indirectly, because token cost is reported inconsistently, or not at all, across the financial-QA literature we survey, and which already falls below our own directly measured figure, though whether HiREC's true FinanceBench-specific cost does as well remains open.</jats:p>

title: Ex-ante Identification of Disruptive Technologies from Patent Text via LLM-Based Semantic Evidence Aggregation

affiliation.name: University of International Business and Economics
University of International Business and Economics

items.abstract: Identifying disruptive technologies at an early stage is important for understanding technological change and anticipating emerging technological trajectories. However, disruptive effects are often observed only after citation patterns, market structures, or industrial configurations have changed. Ex-ante identification therefore requires earlier forms of evidence, and patent text can provide such evidence by recording new technological combinations, functions, and standard-related claims before these outcomes become visible. Existing methods are often limited by delayed evidence or insufficient interpretability. This study proposes LLM-EIDT, a large language model (LLM)-based semantic evidence aggregation framework that transforms patent text into theory-informed evidence of disruptive potential. Rather than treating disruption assessment as a patent-level scoring problem, LLM-EIDT extracts and aligns patent-level semantic signals, applies theory-informed screening, and aggregates the evidence into technology-level themes. We further construct the Ex-ante Disruption h-index (EDh), a technology-level indicator for quantifying and ranking disruptive potential before citation-based disruption becomes observable. Using 14,265 life-science patents from China, we evaluate the framework across three historical five-year windows and compare EDh-based results with the citation-based Disruption h-index (Dh) computed from long-term forward citations. The best-performing domain-adapted LLM configuration achieved an average F1-score of 0.88 and an average normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) score of 0.83, outperforming conventional deep-learning baselines and untuned LLMs. Case analyses show that the aggregated evidence chains explain the early disruptive potential of technological themes. The results suggest that theory-guided LLMs can make patent-text-based technology forecasting more interpretable and empirically testable.

title: Lightweight Semantic Embeddings Enable Redundancy-Sensitive Knowledge Graph Construction for LLM-Based Document Processing

affiliation.name: Fujitsu (United Kingdom)
Fujitsu (United Kingdom)
Fujitsu (United Kingdom)

items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) pipelines for constructing knowledge graphs from long technical documents can be costly because they often process every section independently, even when sections repeat the same semantic content. We propose an ML-augmented Automated Mapping of Data Definitions (AMODD) pipeline that adds a lightweight Semantic Embedding Layer for pre-LLM section deduplication, post-LLM triple clustering and semantic retrieval over the final graph. The layer uses a locally deployed all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence-transformer model to identify near-duplicate sections before extraction, consolidate semantically equivalent graph entities after extraction and rank triples by cosine similarity at query time. We evaluate AMODD using a controlled A/B experiment on synthetic hydrogen-sector regulatory documents with low, moderate and high redundancy. On the non-redundant document, the embedding layer introduced a 6-10% overhead. On moderately and highly redundant documents, it reduced token consumption by 56.7% and 84.9%, LLM calls by 57.7% and 85.4%, and wall-clock latency by 29.9% and 58.1%, while preserving final graph size above a redundancy-adjusted retention bound. Semantic retrieval also improved broad-query coverage over keyword overlap. These results show that lightweight embeddings can make LLM-based knowledge-graph construction redundancy-sensitive rather than document-length-sensitive.

title: Comprehending semantic and syntactic anomalies in LLM- versus human-generated texts: An ERP study
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly proficient at engaging in human-like conversations, it is essential to understand how people process language generated by LLMs compared to language produced by humans. During language comprehension, people interpret incoming linguistic input by integrating it with their world knowledge (e.g., semantic anomalies can elicit an N400 effect in brain potentials) and linguistic knowledge (e.g., syntactic anomalies can lead to a P600 effect). Crucially, people adjust their language comprehension based on the perceived demographic attributes of the speaker, which has been shown to modulate both semantics-sensitive N400 and syntax-sensitive P600 effects. In two ERP experiments, we investigated whether people are sensitive to the fact that LLMs excel in linguistic formulation (i.e., consistently producing grammatically correct texts) but are prone to hallucination (i.e., occasionally generating nonsensical content). Participants were informed that they would be reading texts previously generated by either an LLM or a human. Experiment 1 revealed an N400 effect for semantically anomalous sentences compared to semantically coherent ones. Importantly, the N400 effect was smaller for LLM-generated texts than for human-generated texts. Furthermore, participants who more strongly believed that LLMs possess human-like knowledge exhibited a larger N400 effect. Experiment 2 demonstrated a P600 effect for syntactic anomalies in LLM-generated texts, with the effect being larger for LLM-generated texts than for human-generated texts (and not statistically significant in the latter). These findings suggest that people’s expectations about LLMs’ potential for hallucination and near-perfect grammatical competence modulate the way they comprehend LLM-generated texts. This research highlights the importance of considering perceived language model attributes when studying human language comprehension in the context of AI-generated texts.

title: Semantic State Abstraction Interfaces for LLM-Augmented Portfolio Decisions: Multi-Axis News Decomposition and RL Diagnostics
items.abstract:
<jats:p>We introduce Semantic State Abstraction Interfaces (SSAI): a methodological template for mapping sparse unstructured text into K auditable, named coordinates with neutral defaults on no-news days, designed to separate representation hypotheses from optimisation variance in sequential decision systems. Our contribution is the framework and its evaluation protocol-not a claim that SSAI outperforms denser alternatives.
<div>
 cast) on a US-equity panel (30 NASDAQ-100 names, FNSPID news, 2019–2023 test), and evaluate it across three parallel estimators—direct factor portfolios (SFP/SRF/SCW), supervised ridge forecasters, and RL agents (DP-PPO, SAC)— that share the same fixed ϕ so that signal and optimiser effects can be read off separately.
</div>
<div>
 What the experiments show. The four-factor SFP reaches 307.2% CR / Sharpe 1.067 over 2019–2023. However, this apparent advantage over buy-and-hold (243.6%) does not survive its own controls: SFP underperforms stratum-matched B&amp;Hinevery coverage tercile (Table 3), reverses at ≥0.2% per-trade costs, and the four-factor vs. sentiment-only daily advantage is non-significant (Wilcoxon p=0.556). A data-driven first principal component of the four axes (PC1-SFP) achieves 433.6% CR under the same portfolio rule—126pp above SSAI—and a FinBERTdirect-portfolio baseline achieves 386.3% (Table 5). The honest summary is that the SSAI portfolio advantage is substantially a basket-selection composition effect, and both PC1 and dense neural encodings are empirically stronger ranking signals in this setting.
</div>
<div>
 What the experiments also show. Naively appending sparse LLM columns hurts ridge forecasting; high-conviction semantic tilts and lexical baselines (VADER, TF IDF/SVD) recover price-only Sharpe. The RL block is a diagnostic: DP-PPO trails buy-and-hold; SAC with identical SSAI observations improves Sharpe (1.128 vs. 1.032), isolating algorithm dependence rather than representation advantage. Seed mean Sharpe differences across 21 DP-PPO seeds are non-significant (Wilcoxon p≈0.25–0.31).
</div>
<div>
 Contribution framing. We present SSAI as an interpretability-performance fron tier instrument and a cautionary diagnostic: it characterises the cost of maintaining auditable axes (126pp CR vs. PC1 over five years), shows that RL performance is dominated by algorithm choice rather than representation, and provides a reusable template for separating semantic signal from optimisation noise in other sparse-text decision settings.
</div></jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Groupthink: Causal Analysis and Mitigation of Semantic Convergence in Multi-agent LLM Systems

affiliation.name: Keio University
Keio University
Keio University

items.abstract: When several AI agents work on one open-ended task, such as brainstorming ideas or drafting designs, they usually share drafts so each builds on the others. But sharing also narrows what they produce: asked for many different answers, they return a few similar ones. We tested this across 20 tasks. With the model and sampling fixed, we varied only whether agents could see each other's work. Sharing reduced the semantic diversity of outputs by 5.9%; isolation raised it by 10.3% (p = 0.017, Cohen's d = 0.79). The loss grew with how much was shared, held across five LLMs from three providers (significant in two), and was not explained by input length, drift, or order. We call this pattern Algorithmic Groupthink. It can be countered at the prompt level: under a multi-workflow protocol where sharing cost 31.8% of diversity, one added instruction in the system prompt cut the loss to 5.5% (replicated at n = 20, p = 0.0003, Cohen's d = 1.31), with no loss of quality. The effect appears at inference time, not during training, so developers can adjust diversity by changing how much context the agents share, not by retraining.

                  Decoding dynamic visual information from brain activity remains challenging due to inter-subject neural heterogeneity, limited per-subject data availability, and the substantial temporal resolution gap between fMRI signals (0.5 Hz) and video dynamics (30 Hz). Current approaches face persistent challenges in addressing these temporal mismatches, demonstrate limited capacity to integrate subject-specific neural patterns with shared representational frameworks, and lack adequate semantic granularity for aligning neural responses with visual content. To bridge these gaps, we propose a framework addressing these limitations through three innovations: (1) a Dynamic Temporal Alignment module that resolves temporal mismatches via exponentially weighted multi-frame fusion with adaptive decay coefficients; (2) a Brain Mixture-of-Experts architecture that combines subject-specific extractors with shared expert layers through parameter-efficient tri-modal contrastive learning; and (3) a Multi perspective Semantic Hyper-Anchoring module that resolves cross-subject attention bias via multi-dimensional semantic decomposition, leveraging multimodal LLMs for fine-grained video semantic extraction—enabling the model to match individual attention patterns as different subjects naturally focus on distinct aspects of the same visual stimulus. title: Multi-LLM Semantic Fusion for Context-Aware Traffic Accident Risk Prediction and Personalized Driver Warnings
items.abstract: <jats:p>Traffic accident prevention requires not only accurate risk prediction but also the ability to communicate context-specific warnings to drivers in an understandable and timely manner. This study proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence framework that integrates machine learning–based accident severity modeling, real-time contextual data processing, and large language model (LLM)–driven semantic warning generation for intelligent driver assistance. The proposed framework combines historical accident records, spatial location data, driver-related variables, meteorological conditions, and real-time GPS information to identify high-risk road segments and generate personalized driver warnings.The study consists of three main stages. First, a survey of 576 drivers was conducted to examine risk perception, route familiarity, perceived adequacy of existing traffic safety measures, and acceptance of intelligent warning systems. The findings revealed strong driver demand for dynamic and context-aware warnings, particularly under heavy traffic conditions, unfamiliar routes, and accident-prone locations. Second, accident severity was modeled using machine learning algorithms, with the Random Forest model achieving the strongest classification performance, including a macro-averaged F1 score of 91.72%. Third, the predicted accident risk indicators were integrated with a multi-LLM semantic interpretation layer to transform numerical risk scores and contextual variables into concise, action-oriented, and personalized warning messages.The proposed mobile-based architecture delivers warnings through visual, auditory, and optional haptic interfaces when drivers approach high-risk locations. By combining predictive risk modeling with natural-language explanation and real-time contextual awareness, the framework moves beyond conventional static warning systems and offers a human-centered decision-support approach for intelligent transportation safety. The results suggest that LLM-augmented semantic fusion can improve the interpretability, personalization, and practical usability of traffic accident risk warning systems.</jats:p>

title: PathoScribe: Transforming Pathology Data into a Living Library with a Unified LLM-Driven Framework for Semantic Retrieval and Clinical Integration
items.abstract: <jats:p>Pathology underpins modern diagnosis and cancer care, yet its most valuable asset, the accumulated experience encoded in millions of narrative reports, remains largely inaccessible. Although institutions are rapidly digitizing pathology workflows, storing data without effective mechanisms for retrieval and reasoning risks transforming archives into a passive data repository, where institutional knowledge exists but cannot meaningfully inform patient care. True progress requires not only digitization, but the ability for pathologists to interrogate prior similar cases in real time while evaluating a new diagnostic dilemma.We present PathoScribe, a unified retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) framework designed to transform static pathology archives into a searchable, reasoning-enabled living library. PathoScribe enables natural language case exploration, automated cohort construction, clinical question answering, immunohistochemistry (IHC) panel recommendation, and prompt-controlled report transformation within a single architecture.Evaluated on 70,000 multi-institutional surgical pathology reports, PathoScribe achieved perfect Recall@10 for natural language case retrieval and demonstrated high-quality retrieval-grounded reasoning (mean reviewer score 4.56/5). Critically, the system operationalized automated cohort construction from free-text eligibility criteria, assembling research-ready cohorts in minutes (mean 9.2 minutes) with 91.3% agreement to human reviewers and no eligible cases incorrectly excluded, representing orders-of-magnitude reductions in time and cost compared to traditional manual chart review.By unifying retrieval and reasoning, PathoScribe enables pathologists to move from isolated case interpretation toward data-informed decision-making grounded in institutional precedent. This work establishes a scalable foundation for converting digital pathology archives from passive storage systems into active clinical intelligence platforms.</jats:p>

title: Closing the Social-Semantic Gap: SPSD for Edge-Based Prompt Compression in Cloud LLM Inference
items.abstract: <jats:p>The prefill stage of Large Language Model (LLM) inference is an important and growing contributor to energy cost at cloud scale. In many consumer-support and conversational prompts, a substantial fraction of tokens carry social scaffolding: politeness markers, apologetic preamble, and rapport-building language necessary for human communication but carrying low semantic entropy for machine reasoning. We term this discrepancy the Social-Semantic Gap. We present SPSD (Sentiment Preserving Semantic Distillation), an edge-based pipeline that compresses user prompts using a 4-bit quantised Small Language Model (SLM) before transmission to a cloud-deployed LLM, reducing prefill token cost while maintaining response quality within a pre-specified non-inferiority margin. Evaluation on a 248-prompt corpus using Gemma-2-2B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) as the SLM and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as the cloud-deployed evaluation model yields a mean input token saving of 99.9 tokens per distilled call (t(145)=17.68, p&lt;0.001, d=1.46), with all 146 distilled calls yielding positive savings. Response quality, assessed by LLM-as-judge scoring across 121 pairs, demonstrates non-inferiority of distilled responses within a pre-specified 1-point margin on a 15-point rubric (p=0.010); the judge awarded 43% ties, 28% distilled wins, and 29% raw wins. Cosine similarity was mixed: mean 0.682, median 0.712, with 54.1% of pairs above the 0.70 reference threshold. Safety-critical domains are conservatively routed to passthrough via rule-based gates. Per-call cloud-side prefill energy saving is estimated at 70-270 μWh net of on-device inference cost (~30 μWh), using Luccioni et al. as an order-of-magnitude energy proxy; deployment-scale estimates are illustrative and presented as scenario-based projections. SPSD produces large, statistically significant input-token savings, and the compressed path is non-inferior to the raw path within a pre-specified practical margin.</jats:p>

items.abstract: Pathology underpins modern diagnosis and cancer care, yet its most valuable asset, the accumulated experience encoded in millions of narrative reports, remains largely inaccessible. Although institutions are rapidly digitizing pathology workflows, storing data without effective mechanisms for retrieval and reasoning risks transforming archives into a passive data repository, where institutional knowledge exists but cannot meaningfully inform patient care. True progress requires not only digitization, but the ability for pathologists to interrogate prior similar cases in real time while evaluating a new diagnostic dilemma. We present PathoScribe, a unified retrieval-augmented large language model (LLM) framework designed to transform static pathology archives into a searchable, reasoning-enabled living library. PathoScribe enables natural language case exploration, automated cohort construction, clinical question answering, immunohistochemistry (IHC) panel recommendation, and prompt-controlled report transformation within a single architecture. Evaluated on 70,000 multi-institutional surgical pathology reports, PathoScribe achieved perfect Recall@10 for natural language case retrieval and demonstrated high-quality retrieval-grounded reasoning (mean reviewer score 4.56/5). Critically, the system operationalized automated cohort construction from free-text eligibility criteria, assembling research-ready cohorts in minutes (mean 9.2 minutes) with 91.3% agreement to human reviewers and no eligible cases incorrectly excluded, representing orders-of-magnitude reductions in time and cost compared to traditional manual chart review. By unifying retrieval and reasoning, PathoScribe enables pathologists to move from isolated case interpretation toward data-informed decision-making grounded in institutional precedent. This work establishes a scalable foundation for converting digital pathology archives from passive storage systems into active clinical intelligence platforms.

title: DiG-Align: Distribution-Guided Damage Grounding for Aero-Engine Damage Image-Text Retrieval with LLM-Assisted
items.abstract: <jats:p>Aero-engine damage detection is critical for flight safety and service assessment. Existing learning-based methods mainly focus on classification, detection, or segmentation, producing labels, boxes, or masks, while lacking the ability to retrieve semantically matched maintenance descriptions or historical damage cases. In this paper, we propose Aero-Engine Damage Image-Text Retrieval (named AED-ITR), a retrieval-oriented multimodal task for intelligent aero-engine detection. To support this task, we construct an AeroDamage-ITR dataset, the first LLM-assisted benchmark with structured and quality-controlled image-text pairs covering diverse aero-engine components and damage types. Technically, we propose DiG-Align, a distribution-guided damage grounding framework for AED-ITR. The DiG-Align performs Representation-Calibrated Distribution Alignment (RCDA) to learn damage-aware representations and calibrate batch-wise image-text similarity distributions, strengthening weakly aligned positive pairs under severe visual similarity. It further introduces Explicit Damage Grounding (EDG) to establish sparse token-to-patch correspondences between textual damage cues and local visual evidence, enabling fine-grained and interpretable matching without extra local annotations. Extensive experiments on AeroDamage-ITR demonstrate that DiG-Align outperforms State-of-the-Art image-text retrieval methods, with ablation studies and visualizations verifying the effectiveness of each component.</jats:p>

title: Dynamic User-State Modeling for LLM-Assisted Cultural Heritage Exploration: A Secondary Analysis of Semantic, Behavioral, and Psychometric Signals

items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable open-ended information exploration in digital cultural heritage environments, but uniform conversational support may not accommodate users with different exploration behaviors and curiosity levels. This study develops a dynamic user-state modeling framework that integrates semantic interaction trajectories, behavioral signals, and continuous user characteristics to model individual experience during LLM-assisted cultural exploration. We conducted a secondary computational analysis of an anonymized dataset comprising 132 sessions from 44 participants, with 88 LLM-assisted sessions used for the primary predictive evaluation. A Dynamic Semantic Interaction Representation (DSIR) characterizes local contextual relevance, thematic drift, answer--context semantic alignment, question--answer alignment, novelty, follow-up continuity, and semantic extension. These features are integrated with behavioral observations and continuous Curiosity and Exploration Inventory-II (CEI-II) scores through a low-capacity adaptive gated architecture for joint prediction of System Usability Scale (SUS) and Trust of Automated Systems Test Performance (TOAST-P) scores. Participant-grouped evaluation achieved mean absolute errors of 5.74 for SUS and 0.49 for TOAST-P. Condition-residual analysis showed that substantial predictive information remained after accounting for average interface differences. Behavioral features were particularly informative for usability, whereas semantic coherence contributed more strongly to TOAST-P prediction. Interaction-prefix experiments further showed that approximately half of a session already contained substantial predictive information. These findings provide empirical support for future cultural AI systems that adapt conversational guidance to evolving user states rather than applying uniform assistance.

title: State Consistency in Concurrent LLM Agent Workflows: An Experimental Evaluation of Concurrency Control and Semantic Effect-Time Validation
items.abstract: <jats:p>Context: LLM-based agents increasingly execute state-changing tools against shared transactional systems. Because an agent may read state, reason for hundreds or thousands of milliseconds, and only then attempt an effect, concurrent updates can create stale-state hazards. Objective: We evaluate classical concurrency-control strategies under agent-style read–reason–effect execution and study whether Semantic Validate-Before-Effect (SVBE) can preserve correctness without unnecessarily discarding valid reasoning. Method: We compare six strategies: unsafe execution, pessimistic locking, optimistic concurrency control (OCC), atomic conditional update (CAS), PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE, and SVBE. Experiments span inventory, account, order, and resource-allocation workloads with controlled reasoning delays, contention, retry-budget robustness, extended 1–5 s delays, semantic-survival tests, and live LLM validation. Results: Unsafe execution violated invariants in 65.0% of runs in the primary matrix, while all protected strategies produced zero invariant violations. Increasing reasoning delay from 0 to 500 ms did not increase unsafe violation incidence once concurrent overlap was present. Instead, longer reasoning amplified coordination cost: pessimistic lock waiting increased sharply, while failed OCC and SERIALIZABLE attempts became more expensive. SVBE achieved P95 latency and throughput close to CAS. Across inventory, account, and resource workloads, 75.6% of state changes satisfied semantic preconditions. Live LLM validation produced 299/300 exact contract matches, 113/114 correct no-action decisions, and zero invariant violations across 480 concurrent SVBE operations. P95 read-to-effect windows ranged from 2.06 to 5.15 s. Conclusions: State change does not necessarily imply semantic invalidation. SVBE preserves application invariants through deterministic effect-time validation while avoiding long-held locks during model reasoning and allowing actions to proceed when assumptions remain valid.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>This study introduces the Paper Search Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a unified architecture enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to autonomously search and retrieve academic literature across heterogeneous platforms (arXiv, PubMed, bioRxiv, medRxiv, Semantic Scholar, and CrossRef). By normalizing diverse metadata into a standardized schema, the system facilitates platform-agnostic tool use. We evaluate this infrastructure by tasking GPT-4.1 and GPT-5.1 with generating grounded literature reviews on AI applications in medicine, cybersecurity, and transportation, measuring performance against retrieved abstracts using ROUGE and BERTScore. Results indicate that GPT-4.1 achieves superior semantic and structural alignment, particularly when grounded via CrossRef (BERTScore F1 = 0.881, ROUGE-L F1 = 0.375), outperforming GPT-5.1 across most metrics. While GPT-5.1 demonstrates higher unigram recall (ROUGE-1 = 0.412 on arXiv), it exhibits lower structural fidelity. These findings validate MCP as a robust integration layer for academic RAG systems and demonstrate that standardized tool interfaces enable precise, quantitative assessment of LLM grounding capabilities.</jats:p>

title: SeMiLLa: An R Package and Shiny App for LLM-Assisted Construction and Pre-Empirical Semantic Screening of Psychometric Scales
items.abstract: SeMiLLa is an R package that brings together six phases of LLM-assisted psychometric scale development under a single interface (nine phases and 25 steps in its Shiny app), with 65 public functions and six extensions (version 1.1) grounded in 2022-2026 evidence on LLM use in psychometrics. An offline check on synthetic data showed the four new functions run stably (classification accuracy 100 %, ARI 1.00, explained variance 0.94 with sparsity 0.04 in regularized EFA, and r = 0.99 with lambda = 0.03 in predicted criterion validity), framed as a pre-empirical algorithmic step prior to validation against human responses. The empirical validation spanned three phases: (1) values from SeMiLLa were compared with those reported in nine Spanish validation papers (168 items, n = 4,085) extracted via extraer_psicometria_pdf(); (2) the semantic workflow was compared with uniform calculations over 10 raw OpenPsychometrics datasets (n of about 13,500), five reproduced in canonical Spanish; and (3) the workflow was applied to five Peruvian couple-relationships scales (n = 315 university students). SeMiLLa estimated aggregated reliability with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.04 against raw data and 0.17 against the Peruvian Spanish scales, whereas the correlation between empirical factor loading and within-dimension semantic coherence reached r = 0.59 on raw data. This item-level concordance held in Phase 2 (English) but was lower and even negative in Phase 3 Spanish (Jealousy Scale, r = -0.73). The clustering-consensus item-factor assignment matched the empirical maximum-loading assignment on 74 % of items (mean ARI 0.37), and an adversarial item probing test on WLEIS reached a sensitivity of 1.00 up to four poisoned items. An ordinal robustness analysis supported these results: polychoric reliability was somewhat higher than Pearson (+0.019 to +0.122) without changing the ordering across scales, and a WLSMV CFA showed adequate fit in several scales (e.g., DASS-21, CFI = 0.971). SeMiLLa provides stable estimates of aggregated reliability and item-factor assignment across languages, whereas item-level concordance depends on the conceptual overlap among dimensions and the lexical diversity of items. Consequently, SeMiLLa works as a pre-empirical screening tool, not a substitute for response-based validation.

title: Evidence-Bound Factual Repair in Retrieval-Augmented LLM Answers: Separating Semantic Localization from Deterministic Realization
items.abstract: <jats:p>Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces reliance on parametric knowledge but does not prevent unsupported or contradictory statements. We evaluate a repair pipeline that separates semantic localization from factual realization: a language model selects evidence sentences, while a deterministic program substitutes them verbatim without authority to author replacement text. One frozen pipeline is evaluated against RAGTruth hallucination labels and ExpertQA evidence-grounding labels. Among 889 held-out RAGTruth responses, repair achieved a net reduction of 12 of 32 human-labelled hallucinations (37.50%; exact paired p = 0.0042; 95% CI [18.3%, 56.7%]). Among 731 ExpertQA responses, 26 of 110 reviewed grounding failures were repaired (23.64%; exact paired p = 4.17 × 10⁻⁷). Rationale-blinded second-author endpoint verification found 100% agreement on RAGTruth and 98.84% on ExpertQA (Cohen's κ = 1.000 and 0.977); two ExpertQA disagreements were resolved by consensus. Major completeness loss, defined as a change to the direct answer or protected meaning, occurred in 2.3–2.8% of responses across the two datasets. A zero-additional-cost provenance tool identifies evidence-copied, flagged, and unchecked text.</jats:p>

items.abstract: Microplastic pollution presents significant environmental and health risks, with increasing concern over its presence in aquatic, terrestrial, and atmospheric ecosystems. Despite advances in analytical methods, reliable identification and quantification of microplastics remain challenging, particularly under real-world conditions. Traditional Raman-based methods often struggle with accurate detection due to interference from environmental background materials, such as minerals and biological debris, leading to both overestimation and underestimation of microplastic concentrations. This study introduces a novel framework for microplastic identification by integrating Raman spectra with multimodal semantic features derived from large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional methods relying on raw spectral vectors, the proposed approach combines expert-level semantic descriptors, including peak positions, intensities, widths, and symmetry, with original spectral data to overcome limitations caused by environmental noise and background interference. By employing an attention-based feature fusion strategy, the framework enhances the robustness, accuracy, and interpretability of microplastic detection, ensuring reliable performance across varying environmental conditions and instrument settings. Evaluations on two independent Raman datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in classification accuracy and generalization. External validation on a real-world environmental monitoring dataset containing both plastic and non-plastic samples further confirms the robustness and applicability of the method in open-set screening conditions. In addition to improving classification performance, this study emphasizes interpretability by linking model decisions to observable spectral features, which is essential for expert validation and decision-making. Overall, this work presents an interpretable and scalable strategy for Raman-based microplastic identification, with potential applications in environmental monitoring, recycling systems, and studies of microplastic exposure and health impacts.

title: A Dual-Layer Semantic-Lossless IFC Encoding for LLM-Readable Building Model Interaction
items.abstract: <jats:p>Industry Foundation Classes (IFC) files encode building information in a verbose STEP physical file format that exceeds the context window limits of large language models (LLM), preventing direct AI-driven interaction with building information models. This study proposes a dual-layer semantic-lossless encoding that separates IFC spatial hierarchy from geometric parameters, compresses each layer through domain-specific strategies, and reconstructs the original file on demand. Evaluation of a corpus encompassing five building typologies demonstrates a 7.39x byte-weighted compression ratio and a 53.0x median context reduction in LLM-facing tokens, while SHA-256 hash verification confirms bit-exact roundtrip fidelity. Three commercial LLMs achieved a mean accuracy of 0.993 on structured building information queries against the encoded representation, and a generation pilot produced schema-valid IFC files in 45 out of 45 trials. The proposed encoding enables BIM portfolio archival, offline building information retrieval, and LLM-driven model authoring without requiring commercial 3D modeling tools.</jats:p>

title: Semantic Grounding of Novel Spoken Words in the Primary Visual Cortex
container-title: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
items.abstract: <jats:p>Embodied theories of grounded semantics postulate that, when word meaning is first acquired, a link is established between symbol (word form) and corresponding semantic information present in modality-specific—including primary—sensorimotor cortices of the brain. Direct experimental evidence documenting the emergence of such a link (i.e., showing that presentation of a previously unknown, meaningless word sound induces, after learning, category-specific reactivation of relevant primary sensory or motor brain areas), however, is still missing. Here, we present new neuroimaging results that provide such evidence. We taught participants aspects of the referential meaning of previously unknown, senseless novel spoken words (such as “Shruba” or “Flipe”) by associating them with either a familiar action or a familiar object. After training, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging to analyze the participants’ brain responses to the new speech items. We found that hearing the newly learnt object-related word sounds selectively triggered activity in the primary visual cortex, as well as secondary and higher visual areas.These results for the first time directly document the formation of a link between the novel, previously meaningless spoken items and corresponding semantic information in primary sensory areas in a category-specific manner, providing experimental support for perceptual accounts of word-meaning acquisition in the brain.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Genetic programming (GP) has been widely used in quantitative finance for discovering formulaic alpha factors that can predict asset returns. However, GP often produces overgrown expressions that are difficult to interpret and expensive to evaluate. This paper proposes a large language model (LLM)-assisted pruning framework that reviews expression trees generated by GP, with the LLM acting as a semantic reviewer that flags redundant or financially implausible branches based on structural complexity and contextual reasoning. The proposed method is formalized as a closed-loop Trigger–Evaluate–Decide–Execute (TEDE) process. We present mathematical formulations, algorithmic design, and examples showing how redundant nested functions can be simplified while monitoring predictive performance. Experiments with high-frequency cryptocurrency market data, using DeepSeek-V4-Flash as the semantic engine, show lower expression complexity and higher rubric-based interpretability scores for the pruned symbolic factors. Under the reported test setup, the LLM-pruned configuration has higher Information Ratio (IR) values than the listed baselines and more compact expression trees than the GP baselines.</jats:p>

title: From Coordinates to Context: An LLM-Bootstrapped Semantic Encoding Framework for Privacy-Preserving Mobile Sensing Stress Recognition
items.abstract: <jats:p>Psychological stress is a widespread issue that significantly impacts student well-being and academic performance. Effective remote stress recognition is crucial, yet existing methods often rely on wearable devices or GPS-based clustering techniques that pose privacy risks and lack of human understandable explanations. In this study, we introduce a novel, end-to-end privacy-enhanced framework for semantic location encoding using a self-hosted OSM engine and an LLM-bootstrapped static map for human-friendly feature extraction, and pave a pathway for privacy-aware location data transformation for dataset sharing. We rigorously quantify the privacy-utility-explainability trilemma and demonstrate (via LOSO validation) that our Privacy-Aware (PA) model achieves robust privacy protection without being statistically distinguishable in stress recognition performance from a non-private model. Model explanation analysis highlights that our extracted features, which are user-friendly features, match with psychological literature about stress. In addition, an ablation study on the GeoLife dataset also demonstrates that our privacy framework improves privacy by 2-3 times compared to a non-privacy-aware approach. This suggests that our system can be utilized for the next generation of GPS transformations in open-source datasets for future researchers.</jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The semantic capabilities of large language models (LLMs) have the potential to enable rich analytics and reasoning over vast knowledge corpora. Unfortunately, existing systems either empirically optimize expensive LLM-powered operations with
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">no performance guarantees</jats:italic>
                    , or limit their support to simple batched-inference primitives. We introduce
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">semantic operators</jats:italic>
                    , the first formalism with statistical accuracy guarantees for general-purpose AI-based operations with natural language parameters (e.g., filtering, sorting, joining or aggregating records using natural language criteria). Each operator can be implemented by multiple
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">AI algorithms</jats:italic>
                    , which compose individual model invocations to orchestrate the model over the data. Our programming model specifies the expected behavior of each operator with a high-quality
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">reference algorithm</jats:italic>
                    , and we develop an optimization framework that reduces cost, while providing accuracy guarantees for individual operators. Using this approach, we propose several novel optimizations to accelerate semantic filtering, joining, group-by and top-k operations by up to 1, 000×. We implement semantic operators in the LOTUS system and demonstrate LOTUS' effectiveness on real, bulk-semantic processing applications, including fact-checking, biomedical multi-label classification, search, and topic analysis. We show that the semantic operator model is expressive, capturing state-of-the-art AI pipelines in a few operator calls, and making it easy to express new pipelines that match or exceed quality of recent LLM-based analytic systems by up to 170%, while offering accuracy guarantees. Overall, LOTUS programs match or exceed the accuracy of state-of-the-art AI pipelines for each task while running up to 3.6× faster than the highest-quality baselines. title: A Multi-Level Evaluation Framework for LLM-Based Semantic Feature Engineering in Automated Valuation Models
items.abstract: <jats:p>Automated Valuation Models primarily rely on structured property attributes, often overlooking valuable information embedded in real-estate listing descriptions. This paper presents a multi-level framework that leverages Large Language Models to transform unstructured property descriptions into interpretable semantic meta-features for house price prediction. The framework evaluates both semantic extraction quality and the impact of these features on downstream prediction.Experiments on residential property sales from Hobart and Sydney&apos;s Northern Beaches compare GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1, and Mistral. Semantic features are evaluated against GPT-4o reference annotations and integrated with structured attributes using gradient boosting and random forest models. Results show that GPT-4o-mini achieves the highest semantic agreement and strongest valuation performance, with the largest gains in Sydney&apos;s Northern Beaches. Overall, LLM-derived semantic features provide complementary and interpretable information that improves AVM accuracy and transparency.</jats:p>

title: Hybrid Transformer-Based Recommender System with LLM-Assisted Semantic Modeling for Sequential and Federated Learning

affiliation.name: Indian Institute of Technology Dhanbad

St. Ann's College of Engineering Technology

items.abstract: Sequential recommender systems based on transformers have shown good performance to model the user interaction dynamics, although they usually depend mainly on the interaction data and fail to use rich semantic data that exists in item metadata. This is a major constraint especially in cases of sparsity and cold-start when the interaction histories are not enough to model preference accurately. This paper presents the suggestion of LLMTransRec, a hybrid Transformer-based recommendation model combining collaborative interaction cues, semantic representations generated by pretrained language models, and content-based features into a single model. In order to successfully integrate these heterogeneous modalities, we propose a context-sensitive gating system, which dynamically weighs the contributions of these modalities on the context of the sequence of interactions between a user. We test the suggested framework on a variety of benchmark datasets having different sparsity and richness of content. The experimental findings prove that the model attains stable improvements when compared to strong sequential and graph-based baselines on an integrated sampled evaluation protocol. Other studies, such as ablation analysis and cold-start analysis indicate that semantic features and adaptive fusion can help enhance the robustness of recommendations. On the whole, the findings indicate that the integration of semantic representations into sequential recommendation models is a viable way of improving the performance in the sparse-data context.

title: Deep Fractile Newsvendor Optimization Enhanced by LLM-Based Feature Discovery from Semantic Labels
items.abstract: <jats:p>Retail datasets often contain both numerical features and semantic labels, such as store locations, product names, and dates of sales, that implicitly encode external demand drivers but are typically treated as opaque categorical codes. We propose a Deep Fractile Newsvendor framework that combines decision-focused neural learning with LLM-based feature discovery. On the decision side, rather than training a neural network to predict order quantities directly, we use the empirical mixture distribution (EMD) as a distribution-side prior and the cost-implied critical ratio (fractile) as a decision-side prior. The network with feature input learns only a bounded, dimensionless adjustment around the cost-implied critical fractile, and the resulting adjusted fractile is mapped back through the EMD to obtain the order quantity. This formulation constrains decisions within the historical demand range, reduces scale sensitivity, and discourages large deviations, and is stabilized by Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) regularization in limited-sample settings. On the feature side, an LLM serves as a semantic-to-source mapper: it interprets semantic labels and identifies verifiable external data sources (e.g., a meteorological API), from which numerical features are retrieved. A profit-based selection loop retains only features that improve profit. Across four datasets spanning three countries and three languages, adding quality-checked LLM-discovered external candidates followed by profitbased selection improves validation-period profit significantly when informative semantic labels, such as store locations, dates of sales, and product names, are present. In synthetic-data experiments, our fractile adjustment approach yields lower regret than the tested benchmarks when sample sizes are limited.</jats:p>

title: Synchronizing LLM-based semantic knowledge bases via secure federated fine-tuning in semantic communication
container-title: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: <jats:p>Semantic communication (SemCom) has seen substantial growth in recent years, largely due to its potential to support future intelligent industries. This advancement hinges on the construction and synchronization of robust semantic knowledge bases (SKBs) across multiple endpoints, which can be achieved through large language models (LLMs). However, existing methods for constructing and synchronizing LLM-based SKBs often face numerous security threats, such as privacy leakage and poisoning attacks, particularly when federated fine-tuning is employed to update LLM knowledge bases. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Secure Federated Fine-Tuning (SecFFT) scheme for synchronizing LLM-based SKBs in semantic communication. First, we incorporate homomorphic encryption into SecFFT to ensure the secure synchronization of model parameters. Second, to enhance the trustworthiness of participants against poisoning attacks, we introduce a residual-based access control mechanism, where only participants with low residuals are authenticated to participate in updating the knowledge base. This mechanism is combined with a hash-based message authentication code. Third, we design a self-adaptive local updating strategy to minimize the impact of poisoned model parameters on benign participants, which is crucial for strengthening the robustness of LLM-based knowledge bases against poisoning attacks. Extensive experiments, conducted using four different datasets from the GLUE benchmark, demonstrate that SecFFT can securely synchronize distributed LLM-based SKBs while maintaining high accuracy (98.4% of the performance of the original federated LoRA), with an acceptable additional cost.</jats:p>
